meta.location: The court of king Noah, in the land of Lehi-Nephi
meta.date: ~148 BC (Isaiah 53 quoted entire; Isaiah's oracle ~700 BC)

world_behind.title: A defendant reading scripture at his judges
world_behind.text: Abinadi is under arrest and mid-answer. The priests opened this exchange by quoting Isaiah 52 at him and asking what it meant. What comes back is more Isaiah, and the court has to sit through twelve verses of it.

world_behind.title: Both sides own the book
world_behind.text: Noah's priests could produce Isaiah from memory in open court, which suggests the brass plates' contents were in circulation among the professional class of this colony. Abinadi's charge in the previous chapter was never that they lacked the text. It was that the text was not written in their hearts.

world_behind.title: Isaiah's servant in his own setting
world_behind.text: The passage belongs to a set of oracles in Isaiah about a servant who suffers on behalf of others and is afterward vindicated. Read in Judah, the figure could be taken for the prophet, for a faithful remnant, or for the nation itself. Abinadi will read it of one person, and says so in the next chapter (Mosiah 15:1).

world_behind.title: Temple vocabulary, handed to temple professionals
world_behind.text: "An offering for sin" at verse 10 names a specific class of sacrifice. The men listening administered that system for a living. The verse takes a category from their own work and applies it to a person.

world_behind.title: A century and a half early
world_behind.text: Abinadi is speaking around 148 BC, quoting an oracle from roughly 700 BC, about a death still far in the future for everyone in the room. Nothing in the chapter is presented as a forecast; the grammar mostly treats it as news.

world_behind.title: The chapter break belongs to Isaiah
world_behind.text: Mosiah 13 stops in the middle of Abinadi's sentence and Mosiah 15 resumes his exposition. Sitting between them is one Isaiah chapter, whole, with nothing added before it and nothing appended after. The chapter division follows the boundary of the quotation itself.

world_behind.title: Not the first witness in the record
world_behind.text: Nephi had already written of a Messiah scourged and spit upon, and Benjamin had described blood coming from every pore. Abinadi does not add a newer witness than either. He reaches for the oldest one available to him.

words.text: A thing heard, not a document filed. The word names the message as it arrives in someone's ear, so the question asks about reception: whether anybody took the account in. Abinadi puts that question to a court that has just demanded an explanation of a different passage.

Pleasing appearance, the quality that makes a thing worth looking at. The verse pairs it with "form," removes both, and then adds "no beauty that we should desire him": three words for attractiveness, all negated in one breath. It occurs nowhere else in the Book of Mormon.

To appraise, to set a value on something. It appears twice in two verses and names a mistake both times: "we esteemed him not," then "we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God." The word says nothing about whether the appraisal was correct. That is what lets the chapter record a verdict and then overturn it.

Corrective punishment, the kind a parent or a teacher administers, rather than the sentence a court hands down. The verse says the chastisement of our peace was upon him, which puts the correction on one party and the peace on another. This is its only appearance in the Book of Mormon.

Mute, with no suggestion of stupidity; that insult is much later. The word describes a sheep before shearers, an animal that fails to resist because it does not know there is anything to resist. Applied to a person it names a silence that looks like consent from outside.
A line of descent. The question asks who will name his posterity. Abinadi picks up exactly this question two chapters later and answers it with a list of people.

Goods taken in war and divided afterward. Three chapters earlier Noah's armies came home "rejoicing in their spoil" and grew proud of their own strength on the back of it. Here the strong are on the receiving end of the division.

phrases.term: Yea, even doth not Isaiah say
phrases.text: The whole of Abinadi's own contribution to the chapter, and the phrase occurs once in scripture. It is a question. He is not introducing evidence so much as asking whether the men who quoted Isaiah at him had read as far as the next verse.

phrases.term: As a root out of dry ground
phrases.text: Isaiah has "out of a dry ground." Dropping the article turns a particular patch of dirt into a condition. The image survives the change intact: a shoot with no visible reason to be growing where it is.

phrases.term: Surely he has borne our griefs
phrases.text: Isaiah has "hath borne." The change is small and it lands at the verse where the chapter's central exchange is first stated. The plainer verb makes the line read as a report of something that happened.

Isaiah has the singular, "the iniquity of us all." This is the first of three places where a singular becomes plural (iniquity here, transgression at verse 8, sin at verse 12), and all three sit exactly where the servant is bearing something that belongs to a group.

phrases.term: So he opened not his mouth
phrases.text: Isaiah closes the verse in the present tense, "so he openeth not his mouth," after opening it in the past. Here both halves are past. The verse states the silence twice, and keeping the two statements in one tense makes it a finished account rather than a standing description.

phrases.term: Because he had done no evil
phrases.text: Isaiah has "no violence." This is the chapter's one substituted word, and it widens the claim considerably: violence names a category of act, evil names anything at all. The rest of the verse, including "neither was any deceit in his mouth," stands unchanged.

phrases.term: He shall see the travail of his soul
phrases.text: Isaiah reads "He shall see of the travail of his soul." One dropped word changes what gets seen: the whole of the labor. The clause that follows, "and shall be satisfied," reads differently once a portion becomes a total.

phrases.term: He bore the sins of many
phrases.text: Isaiah has "he bare the sin of many." Both the verb form and the number shift, which makes this the most altered clause in the chapter. It is also the last thing said about the servant before the word "intercession."

verses.label: v. 1–12
verses.title: A short chapter, heavily touched
verses.text: Twenty-four chapters in this volume quote a King James chapter at length. Ranked by the share of verses carrying a real word change, this one is fourth: nine verses of twelve, seventy-five per cent. Ranked by the number of word-level edits it takes to get there, it is near the bottom, with ten. Both facts come from the same cause. The chapter is only twelve verses long, so a handful of single-word substitutions touches most of it, and no long passage anywhere in it is rewritten.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: A quotation turned into a question
verses.text: The King James verse asks two questions and punctuates them as two: "Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?" Seven words are set in front of it here, "Yea, even doth not Isaiah say," and the question mark inside becomes a comma. The whole poem is now the object of Abinadi's own question to the priests, which is the situation he is in. He is not reciting scripture; he is asking men who claim to teach it whether they have read it.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: One tense for both silences
verses.text: The King James verse says the silence twice and uses two tenses: "yet he opened not his mouth," and then "so he openeth not his mouth." Here the second is brought into line with the first, "so he opened not his mouth," and the verse reports one past event instead of a past event and a standing habit. The lamb and the sheep are both untouched. Only the verb that frames them moves.

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: The reason given for the grave
verses.text: The King James gives the reason for the grave among the wicked as "because he had done no violence." This version reads "because he had done no evil," and the substitution widens the claim considerably. Violence is one kind of wrong and can be denied by a man who has done others; evil is the category. The second half of the verse, "neither was any deceit in his mouth," is unchanged, so the pairing now runs from the general to the particular instead of between two particulars.

verses.label: v. 11
verses.title: The preposition that decides how much
verses.text: Isaiah has the servant "see of the travail of his soul," which means he sees some part of it. One word is deleted here and he shall "see the travail of his soul." The travail stops being a supply he draws from and becomes an object he looks at whole. It is the smallest edit in the chapter, and the only one anywhere in it that removes a preposition instead of swapping a noun.

chapter.title: He answers by reading on
chapter.text: The priests quoted Isaiah 52:7–10 and asked what it meant. This reply begins at Isaiah 53:1, the next verse in the scroll. Abinadi does not hunt for a proof text; he picks up where they stopped, which treats their question as a failure to finish rather than a failure to understand.

chapter.title: Six words of his own
chapter.text: "Yea, even doth not Isaiah say" is everything Abinadi contributes here. The remaining twelve verses are quotation. Given the floor in a capital trial, he spends it reading someone else aloud.

chapter.title: The differences are mostly punctuation
chapter.text: Set beside the King James text, this chapter differs at semicolons where Isaiah has colons, at the capitalization of "Lord," and at a scattering of commas. Four differences are not cosmetic: violence becomes evil at verse 9, openeth becomes opened at verse 7, "see of the travail" becomes "see the travail" at verse 11, and three singulars go plural.

chapter.title: Singular to plural, three times
chapter.text: Iniquity, transgression, and sin each turn plural at verses 6, 8, and 12. Every one of the three falls where the servant is carrying something on behalf of a group. The effect is to itemize the load instead of naming it as a single category.

chapter.title: The tenses never settle
chapter.text: Verse 2 looks forward, verses 3 through 9 look back, and verses 10 through 12 swing forward again. An event still a century and a half away is delivered mostly in the past tense, and the record passes over this without comment.

chapter.title: No stable speaker
chapter.text: "Our report," "we hid," "we esteemed," and then "my people" at verse 8 and "my righteous servant" at verse 11. The plural first person is the crowd that got it wrong; the singular is God. Neither one is Abinadi, and the chapter never names either.

chapter.title: The pivot of the trial
chapter.text: Mosiah 11 through 17 runs as a single unit: Noah's court, the charge, the law read out, this chapter, the exposition, the fire. Chapter 13 hands the priests the commandments they were not keeping. Chapter 14 hands them the prophets they were not reading. Chapter 15 tells them who it was about. Law, prophecy, identification, in that order.

chapter.title: The servant passage arrives in two hands
chapter.text: Isaiah's fourth servant oracle opens at Isaiah 52:13 with "my servant shall deal prudently." Those three opening verses appear in this record only in Christ's mouth, at 3 Nephi 20:43–45. Abinadi carries the twelve that follow. No one in the Book of Mormon quotes the passage whole.

applications.title: Read on before you explain
applications.text: The priests asked about a passage and were handed the next passage. When a text is confusing, the cheapest move available is usually to keep reading rather than to reach for a commentary.

applications.title: Check the direction of your accounting
applications.text: The onlookers were right that he was stricken and wrong about who had struck him. When you see someone suffering and an explanation arrives quickly, notice how little that explanation cost you.

applications.title: Notice what a silence is doing
applications.text: The verse states twice that he opened not his mouth. There is a silence that concedes and a silence that refuses to be drawn, and from outside they look identical. Ask which one you are keeping.

applications.title: Straying is one at a time; rescue is not
applications.text: Every one turned to his own way, and the iniquities of all of them landed in one place. Whatever you wandered into by yourself, you will probably not get out of by yourself.

applications.title: Ask who the seed is
applications.text: Abinadi treats "he shall see his seed" as a question with an actual answer and spends the next chapter naming people. Take a promise you find abstract and ask what it would look like if somebody had to produce a list of names.

applications.title: Do not require it to look like anything
applications.text: No form, no comeliness, no beauty that we should desire him. The chapter's opening claim is that the thing worth having did not present as worth having. Audit what you have declined lately on the strength of how it looked.

applications.title: Speak for the group you were counted in
applications.text: He was numbered with the transgressors and then made intercession for them. Where you have been lumped in with people unfairly, one move available is to advocate for them rather than to distinguish yourself from them.

questions.text: What have I asked about without reading the next verse?
Whose face have I hidden from because looking would have cost me something?
When have I explained someone's suffering in a way that conveniently let me off?
Which of my own ways am I currently calling a path?
What do I quietly assume a person's circumstances prove about them?
What labor of mine would I be satisfied to see the whole of?
